author: Elizabeth Dinh
title: How Portland's Nodoguro offers a taste of Toyama, Oregon's sister prefecture - NewsBreak
text:
By Elizabeth Dinh ,
3 hours ago
PORTLAND, Ore. (KOIN) — Portland has a Japanese sister city, named Sapporo, and Oregon’s sister prefecture is Toyama.
Now, you can get a taste of Toyama at a Portland restaurant.
It’s a place that’s been around since 2014, highlighting both Japan and the Pacific Northwest, and it was once again nominated for the highest honor, the James Beard Award.
Located in the historic Morgan Building, which was built in 1913, Nodoguro isn’t obvious from the street. But the intimate space that seats just 24 has garnered national prominence.
“Portland attracted me here because of the ingredients and the environment. Initially, because the terrain is a lot like Japan,” said Ryan Roadhouse, who found Nodoguro along with his wife, Elena.
The couple moved Nodoguro to downtown in 2025.
Inspired by the building’s history, Elena researched 1913 Japanese interiors and architecture, which is reflected in the design.
As for the menu, they visit Japan every year to see their vendors, learn about new ingredients and collect pottery.
“Recently, we were approached by the government of Toyama to put on a really special dinner here. They wanted some of their artisans who make incredible products that are unique to Toyama,” Ryan said. “One of the things that they’re hoping to promote is a special type of Udon Himi Udon.”
Infusing new ideas into his cuisine is something Ryan likes to do. That’s why dining here is an experience, with different acts.
The culinary style at Nodoguro is considered Kaiseki, which features several varying courses that emphasize seasonality.
For Ryan, it’s also important to have both Japanese and Pacific Northwest influences. As he channels his creative side, Ryan’s finding new kinds of influences from being in downtown.
“I think the most important thing was that we felt that if people want downtown to get better and improve and people have to kind of proactively make decisions to be a part of it,” he said.
Ryan likes how the neighborhood gets him closer to the arts, like the Portland Art Museum and the Oregon Symphony.
And for his regulars, he says 90% are locals and that each meal is like a new voyage.
“For us, we feel great because it’s an opportunity for us to kind of help promote Japan in the U.S., help promote the ingredients for like, a real cuisine and real ingredients in Japan with American people,” Ryan said.
Nodoguro also just started doing a version of high tea, paying tribute to award-winning chef Vitaly Paley, who now lives in Hawaii, but used to have a Russian tea service at the Heathman Hotel.
In chef Ryan’s version, which is on Sundays at 2 p.m., the menu goes from savory to lightly sweet, paired with low-caffeine teas.
